turns.speaker: Wang Lung
turns.text: Wang Lung protested that he did not want to hear such talk, that O-lan's condition was already too grave to be thinking of such things, and that he wanted her to rest and recover.

turns.speaker: the maid
turns.text: The maid whispered to Wang Lung that the sweet rice dish was indeed very hot, and that the eight fruits were arranged nicely on the table, just as O-lan had instructed.

turns.speaker: Wang Lung
turns.text: Wang Lung insisted that O-lan must rest and let him care for their son, that he would not have her worrying about such things now.

turns.speaker: the eldest son
turns.text: The eldest son told his mother that he was sure to marry well and provide for her and their father, that she should not worry about such things.

turns.speaker: O-lan
turns.text: O-lan looked at the eldest son with a determined gaze and told him that she knew he was a good boy, but he was still young and needed a wife to take care of him.

turns.speaker: the eldest son
turns.text: The eldest son reassured his mother that he was old enough to take care of himself and that he would not bring shame to the family by remaining unmarried.

turns.speaker: Wang Lung
turns.text: Wang Lung insisted that his son was still young and needed a steady wife to guide him, that marrying well was not just a matter of providing for the family, but also of bringing joy to his son's life

turns.speaker: O-lan
turns.text: O-lan looked at Wang Lung with a hint of sadness and told him that she was not thinking of herself, but of the future, and the family's honor.

turns.speaker: Wang Lung
turns.text: Wang Lung told O-lan that she must not think of the family's honor, but of her own health and well-being, that he would do everything in his power to nurse her back to health.

turns.speaker: O-lan
turns.text: O-lan told the eldest son that she knew it would be a great burden to marry a woman of the household, but it was a tradition that had brought honor to their family for generations

turns.speaker: the eldest son
turns.text: The eldest son explained to his mother that he understood the importance of the family's tradition, but he was not sure if he was ready to take on the responsibilities of marriage yet.

turns.speaker: Wang Lung
turns.text: Wang Lung's voice rose in protest as he told O-lan that he would not have their son married off to some household daughter without his consent, that such a decision was not just O-lan's to make

turns.speaker: O-lan
turns.text: O-lan looked at Wang Lung with a hint of resignation and told him that he had always known how to manage the family's affairs, but now it was time for him to trust her judgment and make the decisions that would secure their family's future

turns.speaker: Wang Lung
turns.text: Wang Lung insisted that his son was still too young to take on the responsibilities of marriage and that he would not allow the decision to be made without his consent.

turns.speaker: O-lan
turns.text: O-lan asked the eldest son to consider the happiness of his future wife, that she would be a part of their family and bring joy and companionship to their household

turns.speaker: the eldest son
turns.text: The eldest son asked his mother if she was feeling better, and if there was anything he could do to help her, his voice filled with concern.

turns.speaker: O-lan
turns.text: O-lan looked at her husband with a hint of sadness and told him that she knew he was worried about her, but she also knew that she had to see the eldest son settled before she passed away

turns.speaker: Wang Lung
turns.text: Wang Lung insisted that O-lan must not exhaust herself by worrying about their son's future, and that he would take care of everything, including finding a suitable wife for their son.

turns.speaker: O-lan
turns.text: O-lan told Wang Lung that she knew he was trying to protect her, but she could not rest until she had seen the eldest son married and settled, as it would be a comfort to her in her final days

turns.speaker: Wang Lung
turns.text: Wang Lung said that he would not rest until the eldest son was married and settled, and that he would do everything in his power to ensure that it happened before O-lan passed away

opening.speaker: O-lan
opening.text: O-lan told Wang Lung that there was another thing she had to attend to before she could die.

opening.speaker: Wang Lung
opening.text: Wang Lung insisted that O-lan should not speak of dying and that it would please him if she did not.

opening.speaker: O-lan
opening.text: O-lan replied that she had to die, for she felt it in her vitals waiting, but she would not die before her eldest son came home and before he wedded this good maid who was her daughter-in-law, and well she served O-lan, holding the hot water basin steadily and knowing when to bathe O-lan's face when she sweated in pain. Now O-lan wanted her son to come home, because she had to die, and she wanted him to wed this maid first, so that she might die easily, knowing that her grandson was stirred into life and a great-grandson for the old one.

opening.speaker: Wang Lung
opening.text: Wang Lung told O-lan that she looked twice as well as they had said and years away from death.

opening.speaker: O-lan
opening.text: O-lan declared that she would see Wang Lung wedded and then she must die.

opening.speaker: O-lan
opening.text: O-lan instructed Wang Lung to sit there and drink the wine and eat the rice of his marriage, for she would see it all and this would be his bed of marriage since she was soon to be finished with it and carried away.

opening.speaker: O-lan
opening.text: O-lan asked if everyone had wine, if the sweet rice dish in the middle of the feast was very hot, if they had put full measure of lard and sugar into it, and if the eight fruits were present.

opening.speaker: O-lan
opening.text: O-lan told Wang Lung that she was now content and that this thing in her may do as it would. She instructed her son to look to his father and his grandfather, and her daughter to look to her husband and his father and his grandfather and the poor fool in the court, there she was. And she told Wang Lung that he had no duty to any other.

opening.speaker: O-lan
opening.text: O-lan said that, even if she was ugly, she had borne a son; although she was but a slave, there was a son in her house.

opening.speaker: O-lan
opening.text: O-lan insisted that no one else could feed Wang Lung's son and care for him as she did. She told Wang Lung that beauty would not bear a man sons.
